# Task: Make a web 3D teaching experiment "Motor and Generator: Take it apart"

Technology stack: Three.js r163+ (ES modules) + native JS/CSS. All models are modeled procedurally. The goal of the picture is "high-end industrial product disassembly film", referring to the explosion shots of Apple product launches, Dyson product cutaway videos, and KeyShot studio renderings.

**Execution order (mandatory)**:
1. Write a brief design (chapter, model list, shot list) and give it to me for confirmation;
2. Use the "shader ball test scene" (see Chapter 3) and take screenshots to confirm the gloss;
3. Set up the camera system and make a 20-second opening shot, export the frame-by-frame screenshots to me to confirm the camera movement;
4. After confirming all the above, complete the implementation.

**Explicitly prohibited**: Neon glow, cyber grid, glass mimic panel, strong bloom, high saturation magnetic induction line, plastic-like metal, crude model made of squares and cylinders, card-style instrument panel, linear interpolation mechanical mirror movement, camera teleportation, lens shake and pause.

---

## Chapter 1 Gloss: Metal must be "as bright as real"

### 1.1 Rendering pipeline (the most common mistakes are here)
- Renderer settings: `outputColorSpace = SRGBColorSpace`, `toneMapping = NeutralToneMapping` (Khronos PBR Neutral, product rendering color is the most accurate; fall back to AgXToneMapping when unavailable), `toneMappingExposure` is adjusted between 1.0–1.3.
- EffectComposer's render target must use `HalfFloatType` (HDR), so that the highlight can exceed 1.0 and Bloom can only capture the true highlight point.
- **The last Pass in the post chain must be OutputPass**, where tone mapping and sRGB conversion are done. Without it, the whole picture would look gray and flat.
- Anti-aliasing: composer render target is turned on `samples: 4`; high-end devices can add SMAA. Pixel ratio upper limit 2.

### 1.2 The metal background color must use true reflectivity (no darkening allowed)
The "dark" part of the metal comes from the black surroundings it reflects, not the base color. The background color is given according to the physical F0 value, and the following are the sRGB values:
| Material | Background color | metalness | roughness | Remarks |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Polished steel (shaft) | `#c9cbcd` | 1 | 0.08–0.12 | To clearly reflect the shape of the light strip |
| Brushed aluminum / stamped steel shell | `#d6d8da` | 1 | 0.32 | `anisotropy 0.7`, brushed in circumferential direction |
| Sandblasted cast aluminum (end caps) | `#cfd1d3` | 1 | 0.48 | Fine noise roughness map, range 0.4–0.56 |
| Brass commutator | `#f2d9a0` | 1 | 0.22 | `anisotropy 0.6`, along the direction of rotation; brush contact zone roughness 0.1, brighter |
| Enameled copper wire | `#eaa27c` | 1 | 0.28 | `clearcoat 1`, `clearcoatRoughness 0.05`; add varnish to the bottom copper to produce double-layer highlights |
| Silicon steel sheet (with insulating coating) | `#9a9ea3` | 0.85 | 0.4 | A thin dark line on each piece along the axial direction; end stamping edge roughness 0.2 brighter |
| Balls / Bearing Rings | `#d0d2d4` | 1 | 0.06 | Small, sharp highlights |
| Nickel-plated neodymium magnet | `#d8dadc` | 1 | 0.18 | |
| Ferrite magnet | `#3b3d40` | 0 | 0.7 | Non-metal matte; only low saturation marking paint is applied on the pole surface, N `#b5534a`, S `#4f74a8` |
| Mica flakes | `#3a2614` | 0 | 0.55 | |
| Carbon brush | `#2a2a2c` | 0 | 0.85 | |
| Plastic parts | `#1d1f22` | 0 | 0.5 | clearcoat 0.15 |
- `envMapIntensity` is set to 1.2–1.5 for metals and 0.8–1.0 for non-metals.
- The drawing direction is realized with MeshPhysicalMaterial's `anisotropy` + `anisotropyRotation` (or anisotropyMap); the UV of the cylindrical part must be expanded along the circumference, otherwise the drawing direction will be wrong.
### 1.3 Roughness must vary (this is the source of "realism")
Each metal needs a procedurally generated roughness map (Canvas, 1024², anisotropy 8), consisting of three layers:
1. **Main Texture**: Brushed (thousands of thin lines with random grayscale length) or sandblasting (fine noise);
2. **Low-frequency patches**: Use 2-3 large-scale noises to make the roughness fluctuate ±0.06, simulating traces of hand touching and wiping;
3. **Sparse Thin Scratches**: 20–60 short, bright, thin lines per texture, with random lengths and random directions.
In addition: the wear areas such as the commutator plate contact belt and the bearing raceway should be smoother; the corners should be slightly rough.
### 1.4 Bevel (it determines where the highlight falls)
**All sharp edges** must be rounded with a radius of 1–3% of the part size, in at least 3 segments, with smooth transitions from normals. Without chamfers, the edges won’t catch the highlights and the whole part will look like a CG block. Use LatheGeometry for turned parts (rotating shaft, commutator, end cap), and draw chamfers directly on the contour line; use ExtrudeGeometry for extruded parts, with `bevelEnabled` and `bevelSegments ≥ 3`.
### 1.5 Environment and lighting: large area of pure black + a few bright lights
Metal reflects what it reflects, so the **environment must be extremely contrasting**: 90% pure black, 10% very bright, soft-edged light.
- **Environment Map**: Use PMREMGenerator.fromScene to bake a studio with `sigma` set to 0 to retain sharp reflections.
- Room: reverse sphere, color `#050607` (close to pure black).
- Lights: Use a plane with a gradient texture (bright in the center, 20% soft falloff at the edges), multiplied by a high brightness factor with a MeshBasicMaterial. The HDR brightness needs to be enough so that the metal will be bright.
- Large softbox on top: 10×4, color `#f4f1ea`, brightness ×8, position (0, 9, 3);
- Left rear long light strip: 0.8×12, color `#d4e3ff`, brightness ×14, position (-7, 2, -5), placed vertically, pulling out a cold long highlight on the cylindrical piece;
- Thin light strip on the right rear: 0.4×10, color `#fff2e0`, brightness ×12, position (7, 3, -4), giving warm edges to copper and brass;
- Front low-position weak reflector: 6×1.5, color `#ffffff`, brightness ×2, position (0, -1, 8), leaving a light highlight on the downward facing surface;
- The rest of the environment remains black. Black itself is "negative light", and the dark bands on the metal are formed by it, making the dark bands look sharp.
- **RectAreaLight** (real-time, movable, used to generate sliding highlights): initialize RectAreaLightUniformsLib, put 2 blocks:
- A light: 0.3×3, intensity 18, color `#ffffff`, placed vertically on the left rear of the subject;
- B light: 2×0.4, intensity 10, color `#ffe9d0`, placed horizontally on the upper right side of the subject.
- **DirectionalLight main light**: only responsible for projection, intensity 1.2, shadow map 2048, `radius 4`, shadow camera close to the subject.
- **HemisphereLight**: intensity 0.15, sky color `#d7dde6`, ground color `#121110`, only used to hold the dark parts.
- **Highlights must move**:
- During standby, the A light slowly sweeps back and forth across the subject along an arc, with a cycle of about 14 seconds;
- Each time the camera switches, `scene.environmentRotation.y` rotates 15–30% with the camera azimuth angle, allowing the reflection to slide with the lens;
- The opening "Light Sweep Appearance": the main body starts from completely black, a light strip sweeps from left to right, and the metal is lit up in turn, which takes about 2.4 seconds.
### 1.6 Ground
- Use Reflector, the resolution is 1/2 of the canvas, and do 9 sampling blurs in the shader. Ground background color `#0b0c0e`, Reflection Blend 0.22, radially decaying to 0 with distance from the subject.
- Add a soft oval directly below the subject to touch the dark spot.
- Do not put any grid or text on the ground.
### 1.7 Late chain (fixed order)
1. RenderPass (HDR, MSAA).
2. **GTAOPass**: radius is 2–3% of the body diameter, `thickness 0.8`, `distanceExponent 1.5`, `samples 12`; noise reduction parameters `lumaPhi 10`, `depthPhi 2`, `normalPhi 3`, `radius 5`, `rings 2`, `samples 12`; blending strength 0.8.
3. **Contour Pass** (read GTAO’s depth and normal):
- 4 neighbor samples; the depth jump is calculated with the relative value `(z - zn) / -z`, and only the far edge is traced after `smoothstep(0.012, 0.04)`;
- Normal jump multiplied by 0.45;
- Thread color `#07090a`, mechanical body strength 0.2, schematic coil strength in principle mode 0.5.
4. **Bloom**: threshold set to 1.0 (HDR value, only specular highlights and glowing elements exceed it), strength 0.25, radius 0.35. The goal is to have a small, bright "flash point" on the steel ball and polished shaft, not the entire piece to shine.
5. **Color Pass**:
- Light S-curve `mix(c, c*c*(3-2c), 0.14)`;
- The highlights are slightly warm and the shadows are slightly cold, each about ±0.008;
- Vignetting strength 0.45;
- Dark film grain 0.015.
6. BokehPass (only enabled in close-up, see Chapter 2).
7. **OutputPass** (required).
**Adaptive Downgrade**: When the frame rate continues to be lower than 45, the following processing is performed: GTAO and Contours → Reflection down to 1/4 → Bloom → RectAreaLight down to 1 block → Pixel Ratio → Shadows.

## Chapter 2: Mirroring: Shooting like a photographer, not two-point interpolation
### 2.1 Camera system (build this first, then create content)
Write a CameraDirector to manage three modes uniformly:
- **Lens Mode (Shot)**: Press the shot list to play the preset shot;
- **Follow mode (Follow)**: The camera tracks a target, such as a selected part or a rotating coil;
- **Free mode (Free)**: User operates with OrbitControls.

Camera status = camera position, gaze point target, focal length fov, roll roll, focus distance focus. The five quantities are interpolated independently.
**Data structure of lens**:

- `path`: the camera path points of the Catmull-Rom spline (at least 3 points, ensuring an arc);
- `target`: gaze point path (can be a fixed point or a spline);
- `fov`: starting and ending values;
- `roll`: starting and ending values;
- `dur`: duration;

- `ease`: ease;

- `focus`: focus target;
- `hold`: the residence time after settling;

- `onSettle`: Event triggered after settling (subtitles, annotations).
**Interpolation rules**:

- **Focus leading, camera following**: The gaze point is eased about 15% faster than the camera position, imitating the photographer who first turns his head and then moves his body.
- ** Use easeInOutQuint for large-scale lens movement, and easeInOutCubic for small-scale movement. Linear interpolation is strictly prohibited. **
- **Speed Continuous**: When the shot is interrupted, it will smoothly transition from the current position and current speed to the new shot (transition with critical damping spring for about 0.4 seconds). It cannot restart from a standstill, let alone skip frames.
- **Roll**: Add an inclination of no more than 1.5° when moving along an arc, and return to normal after reaching it, imitating a rocker arm.
- **Focal Length Breathing**: When the lens is pushed in, the FOV is simultaneously narrowed by 2–4°, and when the lens is pulled in, the FOV is relaxed to increase the sense of depth.
- **Speed ​​limit**: The camera angular speed does not exceed 35°/s, and the translation speed does not exceed 0.8 times the diameter of the subject/s.
- **Settling**: After the camera settles, it pauses for 0.4–0.8 seconds before subtitles and annotations fade in. Subtitles never appear at the same time as camera movements.
**Handheld micro-movement**: During the stay in Shot and Follow modes, extremely light Berlin noise is superimposed on the camera position and gaze point: the amplitude is 0.15–0.25% of the observation distance, the frequency is about 0.15–0.3Hz, and the phases of the two components are different. The nudge will fade out as soon as the user starts the operation. This item is small, but it can make the picture "come alive".
### 2.2 Composition
- Place the main body near the three-point line, leaving negative space for the title in the lower left corner and the data on the right.
- When the sidebar or drawer is open, use `camera.setViewOffset` to pan the screen instead of moving the camera. The position of the subject in the picture is adjusted accordingly, and the perspective remains unchanged.
- Use a slight elevation angle for the protagonist lens: the camera is slightly lower than the center of the subject and looks upward 5–10° to make the subject appear thick and powerful; use a 25–35° overhead view for the explanation lens.
- Each shot must have bright parts, dark parts and highlights at the same time; the reflection of the light strip on the metal must be visible when positioned. Don’t choose an angle that makes the subject look dead.
### 2.3 Lens language (the following shots must be made, and each one must be written clearly in the shot list)
1. **Black point light sweep debut**: A completely black opening, a light strip sweeps across, the outline of the subject is highlighted in turn, and then the camera slowly advances about 15% from a low position. Approximately 5 seconds total, with citation in italics and serif.
2. **Surround display**: Make a half circle around the main body along an arc of about 140°, slightly raise it, and roll at the same time. The reflection of the lamp flows on the housing.
3. **Explosion Disassembly**: While the parts are separated along the axis, the camera is pulled back and raised by about 20°, and the FOV is widened by 4°, ensuring that all parts are within the frame throughout the process. Parts fly out sequentially in assembly order, with a delay of 80–120 milliseconds for each part, with slight deceleration rebound; the screw rotates before exiting.

4. **Tile display (knolling)**: Cut from the explosion state to the orthogonal perspective (FOV reaches 18°, the camera rises directly above). All the parts fly to the ground and are arranged in a neat grid, with thin line markings appearing under each part. This is a very classic shot in product films.
5. **Macro focus transfer**: Push to close-up of commutator and brush, FOV 18–22°, open depth of field. The focus is pulled from the commutator to the carbon brush, which takes about 1.2 seconds, and the background is defocused into a soft spot.
6. **Parallel Sliding**: The laminate stacked against the silicon steel sheet moves laterally, and the lamination line slides across the screen, forming a parallax between the foreground and the background.
7. **Section advancement**: The section plane is slowly advanced from the surface of the casing to the central axis, and the camera moves sideways simultaneously to keep the section facing the lens.

8. **In-situ transition (real machine → principle model)**: The camera does not move, the real parts fade out, and the schematic coil and magnetic pole fade out, both sharing the same corner. The camera then slowly zooms in on the coil.
9. **Follow rotation**: When the coil rotates, the camera follows it at an angular speed of 0.3 times, making the coil appear to rotate slower and easier to read in the picture. Users can turn off following.
### 2.4 User free operation
- OrbitControls: `enableDamping`, `dampingFactor 0.06`, `rotateSpeed 0.55`, enable cursor-centered zoom; limit pitch angle and zoom range.
- Double-click a part: Calculate the appropriate distance based on its surrounding sphere, use a 1.2-second arc to push the camera over and align it, and the background part will darken.
- The camera does not rebound after letting go; after 8 seconds of inactivity, lens micro-motion and highlight sweep will fade in again.
- Each chapter provides a "reset perspective", which allows you to go through an arc and return to the default lens of the chapter. Teleportation is not allowed.

## Chapter 3 Acceptance Method (both luster and mirror movement must speak for themselves with evidence)
### 3.1 Shader test scene (must be completed before modeling and let me confirm)
- Under the final studio lighting, make a chamfered test piece for each material in the table above and arrange them in a row: one each for a sphere, a cylinder with chamfers, and a box with chamfers.
- Take 3 pictures: front, 45°, low camera angle.
- Check items one by one:
- The shape of the light strip can be clearly seen on the steel balls and polished shaft;
- The highlight of a brushed piece is an elongated band rather than a dot;

- The copper wire has a double layer of high gloss (varnish layer and copper layer);

- Each metal piece has both a nearly pure black dark band and a very bright highlight band;

-Nothing looks like gray plastic.

If it's not up to standard, adjust the lighting and environment first, then the material, and finally the exposure.
### 3.2 Mirror operation acceptance
- Export frame-by-frame screenshots of the opening 20 seconds using a virtual clock at a fixed 60fps step (one every 6 frames to create a contact sheet).
- Simultaneously record the camera speed and angular speed of each frame into a graph. The curve must be smooth and continuous: no spikes, no jumping to zero, no exceeding the speed limit.
- Interruption test: trigger another lens in the middle of the camera movement to check whether the speed curve is continuous.

### 3.3 Self-examination of screenshots of the finished film

After each chapter is completed, check it according to the standards of 3.1. Also check: whether there are contact shadows between parts; whether there are reflections on the ground; whether magnetic lines of induction are restrained; whether there are card panels or neon lights in the picture.

## Chapter 4 Model Details (Engineering Level)
- The enameled wire is modeled turn by turn, and a real coil cross-section is wound along the slot; the end must have a bulge, a tie and a lead wire, and the lead wire is welded to the hook of the commutator piece.
- Rotor core: real groove shape, optional number of grooves (3 / 5 / 12 grooves), with inclined grooves; lamination lines visible.
- Commutator: real number of pieces, with mica seams between the pieces; the brush is installed in the brush holder, and there is a compression spring behind it.
- Shell: mounting holes, screws, etched nameplate (model, rated voltage, speed), ventilation holes, solder joints.
- Bearing: ball bearing with cage; circlip and keyway are added at the end of the rotating shaft.
- Bevel all sharp edges (see 1.4). All objects are modeled with reasonable real-life sizes (small motor diameter is about 30–40mm, unified in millimeters, or scaled as a whole), otherwise the parameters of the lights and AO will be invalid.
## Chapter 5 Scientific Visualization (Restrained Overlay)

- **Magnetic induction line**: extremely thin pipeline, color `#9fc3e6`, transparency 0.5, with a slow-flowing dotted line texture along the N→S direction, which must pass through the magnetic steel and the iron core. The stronger the magnetic field, the denser the lines and the faster they flow. Magnetic field lines do not participate in Bloom.
- **Current**: Warm-colored small light spots `#ffcf8a` flowing along the wire. The density and brightness of the light spots are proportional to the size of the current; the direction of the light spots must be visibly flipped at the moment of reversal.
- **Force**: White matte solid arrow, the length is proportional to the force.
- **Brush Sparks**: Tiny warm white particles, the higher the speed, the more obvious they are, but be restrained.
- **Cutting**: Use clippingPlanes to cut and stencil to block. Sections are colored according to material and given a very light 45° hatch.
- **Focus**: When a part is selected, the remaining parts are reduced to 15% brightness and desaturated.
- **High Speed ​​Rotation**: At high speed, angular motion blur is added to the commutator segments and notches.
## Chapter 6 Interface (Editorial Documentary HUD)

- Page background color `#040507`; main text color `#f2f4f7`, main text `.78`, secondary `.5`, weakest `.3`, thin line `rgba(220,228,240,.16)`; the only accent color is ice blue `#6fb2e6`.

- Font: Sans serif `"Helvetica Neue", "Noto Sans SC", "PingFang SC"`, title weight 200–300; use italic serif `"Cormorant Garamond"` for embellishment.
- An enlarged and thin font title in the lower left corner, a kicker with widened word spacing above it (e.g. `04 - DC MOTOR / TEARDOWN`), and a line of italic citations below (e.g. "Faraday, 1831").
- Place a right-aligned digital stack on the right side: speed, current, electromotive force, torque.
- Waveform diagram: SVG thin line, no background frame, with a vertical line that moves synchronously with the rotor angle; the neutral plane and reversal point are marked with dotted lines.
- The control is made into "text link + 1px slider". Parts are marked with leader lines, and labels follow the projected position and prevent overlap. Tips for making movie subtitles at the bottom. Pad radial gradient scrim behind text.

- No card, no frosted glass, no shadows. In the vertical screen of the mobile phone, the 3D area accounts for more than 60% of the screen, and the explanations are stored in the bottom drawer.
- Optional: Use WebAudio to synthesize motor sound (the fundamental frequency changes with the speed, superimposing commutation harmonics and brush noise), muted by default.
## Chapter 7 Teaching Content
Corresponding to "Electromotor, Magnetism and Electricity" in junior high school and "Electromagnetic Induction, Alternating Current" in high school, the interface does not indicate the academic level. Core concept: dismantle the real machine to see the structure, the principle model to see the essence, and switch between the two in situ.
1. **Complete machine appearance and disassembly**: Understand the casing, stator magnets, rotor core, windings, commutator, brushes, bearings, and rotating shafts.
2. **Why does the energized coil rotate**: Left-hand rule, the effective side is stressed, and the torque changes with the rotation angle; the coil stops at the equilibrium position, which leads to the commutator.
3. **Commutator**: The moment when the slow discharge current reverses. The number of commutation plates is adjustable (2 / 3 / 5 / 12), and the torque ripple curve becomes smooth accordingly. The number of slots and the number of plates of the real machine change simultaneously.
4. **Factors affecting speed and steering**: voltage, magnetic field, number of turns, direction reversal, and back electromotive force (the current light spot becomes thinner when the speed increases).
5. **Magnetic electricity**: right-hand rule; neutral plane; e = E_m·sinωt, E_m = NBSω. There are four sliders for rotation speed, magnetic field, number of turns, and area, each of which changes the waveform and image at the same time.
6. **AC and DC generator**: Slip rings and commutators can be interchanged, and the waveforms of sinusoidal AC and pulsating DC can be compared in real time; then disassemble a real alternator.

7. **Expansion**: Brushless motor, three-phase generator (the three sets of coils are 120° apart).
8. **On-site testing**: Click in 3D, judge the direction, select the waveform, and use animation playback to explain after judging the score.
**Principle**: Every slider and switch must produce a visible change in the 3D image.
**Physical requirements**: Use the simplified DC motor equation U = E + IR, E = kω, T = kI, and take the parameters as real small motors (3–12V, thousands of rpm). The corners are strictly synchronized with the waveform. Write unit tests for the following relationships: the neutral plane electromotive force is zero; E_m is proportional to N, B, S, and ω; the direction of the torque remains unchanged before and after commutation.

<inputs>
Ask me the following 3 things: the 8–12 UI components the shape transforms into (e.g. a button, a loading indicator, a music player, a volume slider, an on/off switch, tabs, a graph, a search box opened with ⌘K, a toast notification that appears briefly), whether the colors are pure black and white or one accent color, and a royalty-free song around 120BPM (a tempo of 120 beats per minute) (e.g. Mixkit, free for commercial use).
</inputs>

<direction>
Refined UI motion at a level that would be featured on "Dribbble," the portfolio site for designers. There is only one shape, and never cut between scenes. Express every state through motion where the same single shape changes form while changing its size, corner radius, and color, and swap the contents with a short blur in between. The cursor triggers every change with real clicks and drags. The background is a warm light gray, components are white and black, on-screen text is in Japanese, the Japanese font is Noto Sans JP, and Latin letters, numbers, and symbols use Geist (one font family). Make all motion natural, "spring"-like movement, with overshoot (bounce-back) kept very slight. The camera zooms so that each state fills the screen. Make the last frame the same as the first frame so it loops.
Forbidden: bouncy motion, particle-scattering effects, glowing bloom, gradients on components, icons with inconsistent stroke widths, dead pauses where nothing happens, and anything that looks template-like in general.
</direction>

<structure>
120BPM, 7 bars (about 14 seconds), something happens on every beat.
Button → loading indicator → check mark → iPhone Dynamic Island-style display → music player whose play/pause icon morphs smoothly → drag the playback bar's knob to scrub the playback position → transforms into a volume slider (stretches like rubber when dragged past the max) → on/off switch toggles on the beat → the switch knob becomes a liquid-moving tab selection indicator → the tabs open into a graph that draws its own line (a tooltip appears on hover) → folds into a ⌘K search box → type to filter suggestions → Enter → a toast notification flashes briefly → back to the button.
</structure>

<build>
1. One HTML file, square 1440x1440. Compute every visual from time inside seek(t) (a function that, given time t, determines the screen at that moment). Use no CSS transitions (automatic animation features) and no timers, and carry no state over between frames.
2. Make the "spring" motion a form that can be solved directly by formula (closed-form step response). For values whose target changes many times, sum the motions computed one per change. That way, the value is always determined by time alone.
3. For the tab selection indicator, drive the left and right edges with separate springs so the leading edge in the direction of travel stretches ahead of the trailing edge. Use the same technique for the switch knob.
4. Drags are direct manipulation: while the cursor is pressed, compute the value from the cursor position. On release, spring back from that position.
5. Analyze the song with numpy (a computation tool) to find the beat positions, and start from the downbeat of a bar. Place interaction sounds at the measured sound peak positions.
6. Render with Playwright (a tool that automates a browser and exports the screen as images). Export 4 sub-frames per frame, layer them with ffmpeg's (a tool for making videos) tmix to apply motion blur (motion trails), and make it 60fps.
7. Before exporting the whole thing, export just one frame per beat to check. Fix anything off-beat, cramped, or hard to read.
</build>

<gotchas>
Never put will-change (a browser rendering setting) on elements that get scaled by the camera. If you do, the text gets blurry. Give each piece of text that swaps inside a shape-changing box its own dedicated enter/exit timing (to prevent overlap). Make the last frame match the first frame exactly, including the cursor's position and velocity. Otherwise, the loop will stutter.
</gotchas>

<start>
First ask me for the inputs, and before writing any code, show me the per-beat state list.
</start>

- Use cartoon grading for coloring (MeshToonMaterial plus 3rd to 4th level gradient map), with three types of lights: main light, sky light, and graded color outline light.
- Use post edge detection for strokes: render normal map + depth map, then use shader to draw lines. The outer contour is thick, the interface between parts is thin, and the thickness is consistent throughout; in addition, 1.5 times oversampling and multi-sampling anti-aliasing are performed.
  Don't use the "enlarged black backside" type of stroke, as that will cause uneven thickness and breakage at the corners.
  The threshold for depth judgment should be relaxed, and joints should be judged mainly by normal lines, otherwise fine diagonal lines will appear on the surface when viewed diagonally.
- The moving parts need to move realistically, such as the box lid opening around a hinge and the medal rotating around the vertical axis.
- When in standby, the main body slowly rotates left and right, allowing people to see the sides and thickness, while floating slightly up and down; there should be a soft projection that changes with height under the feet.

- Lines are divided into thicknesses: thick outer contours and thin internal structural lines.
- Each character or object should have its own expression and posture, do not share the same face for everything.
- Draw projections on the feet to let the subject "stand" in the picture; distinguish the patterns according to attributes for the background, and do not use the same set of radiation lines.

[Rhythm of performance: five stages, none of which can be missing]
1. Preparation: The main body floats on standby. It shakes every few seconds to indicate that you can click it. A "click" prompt is displayed at the bottom.
2. Upgrade: Each time you click, the main body jumps up, spins around in the air, flattens and rebounds when it lands; at the same time, it switches to the color of the next level, flashes a light, emits a circle of particles, and the title is updated.
3. Accumulation (about 1 second): The main body shakes more and more violently, light shines through the gaps, the surrounding particles are sucked toward the center, and the sound effect continues to rise; at the last moment, it is suddenly crushed.
4. Explosion: a flash of white light spreading outward from the explosion point, screen vibration, camera push forward, multi-layer shock wave, slender streamer burst, flashing star points, gold coins and gems (with rotation). High level bursts are significantly stronger. Use the ribbon only once at the climax, do not fill the screen with ribbons.

3D TUTORIAL VIDEO "OFFSIDE? YOU'LL SEE WHY."

Create a roughly one-minute video in Czech that will clearly explain to children aged 10-12 when it is offside, when it is not and why. Visually, it is supposed to act like a TV broadcast or EA Sports FC: a real stadium, believable players with movement from motion capture and VAR analysis right on the pitch. The interpretation must work without spoken commentary, the pace should allow you to comfortably read the text and understand the situation. Deliver the finished MP4 as well as an editable project.

1. TECHNOLOGY AND PROCEDURE

Character scene in Three.js, captions and player names as HTML/CSS layer above the canvas. Render the video offline: Node.js and Puppeteer open the page in Chrome with the GPU, renderFrame(t) sets the entire image by time, and pipes frames at n / 30 times to FFmpeg. No real-time screen recording. The state of the scene is a pure function of time, so jumping to any instant will return the same image. One timeline controls chapters, skips, stops, subtitles and audio. Sound (subtle music, stadium atmosphere, passing noises, silence during analysis) synthesize in Python. Output: 1920 × 1080, 30 fps, H.264 + AAC; quality master and a smaller version to share. Store all assets locally and only with a CC0 or free-to-use license; write down sources

2. PLAYERS AND ANIMATIONS

Assembly characters from MakeHuman (CC0): multiple body variants, skins and hairstyles, jerseys, shorts, boots and cleats put on as clothing layers, eyes and eyebrows. Simplify the skeleton to a game rig and deform the player with smooth scales. The jerseys will get numbers, fabric material and trims; both formations and goalkeepers must be distinguishable at first glance.

Take motion from real motion capture (CMU Motion Capture Database) and map it to the skeleton: walk, trot, run, walk behind, rest stances, goalie stance, and soccer kicks. Mix the cycles according to the actual speed of the player, while uniting the legs in the same phase of support. Keep the footrests in place with inverse kinematics, the feet must not slide, float or drive into the grass, and the knees must not break back. He places the kick so that the kicker hits the ball exactly at the moment of the pass. The reception of the ball is handled with the open inside of the foot, the ball must not pass through the boot. During the out, the player holds the ball with both hands. After the kick, the player makes a smooth run, never spinning on the spot. Head and torso follow the ball but without jerking. Freeze both the player and the ball when the action is stopped, and resume with the exact same pose.

3. STADIUM, LIGHT AND CAMERA

A pitch with mowing stripes and correct lines, goals with a net, corner flags. Around the two-story stadium with packed stands, waving flags, photographers, organizers and cameras on the line; LED panels with abstract graphics only, no texts, logos or advertisements. Take the sky and reflected light from HDRI. Place the sun behind the opposite stand so that the shadows are directed towards the spectator, parallel to the offside lines and the players have illuminated outlines. Postprocessing: supersampling, contact shading, soft bloom, cinematic color mapping, sharpening and color grade; when you freeze the image, slightly blur the background, the players, ball and graphics will remain sharp. Add motion blur from multiple subframes.

The main camera is a relay camera from the grandstand with a long focal length: a flatter perspective and the opposite grandstand at the top of the image. The VAR analysis is a smooth zoom on the decisive players, no sharp cuts. Both the passer and the receiver must remain engaged. Shoot the car and the corner from a low camera near the field.

4. SCENARIO

Eight short chapters, each with one new idea: the right lead; same action with clear offside; same level (hands and arms not counted); positioning behind the ball; run-in from own half; two attackers, only one of whom is in an offside position and the ball goes to the other; straight car and straight corner. Rhythm: short action → stop exactly at the pass → graphic explanation → finish with a verdict. In the chapter with two attackers, show in freeze sequence first the player in an offside position, then the teammate who is not offside, and finally both with a clear verdict "This is not offside" and the reason. Check the regularity according to IFAB Law 11. The main attackers are named Vašek and Karel; an assistant referee stands on the boundary line, who raises the flag only in the event of a true offside.

5. VAR GRAPHICS AND TEXT

Lines across the field are drawn from the actual decisive body part (everything except the arms counts), with a vertical projection and visible point. Blue indicates the penultimate opponent, red offside, green the correct position and allowed exceptions, amber the ball and the path of the pass. The space between the lines is a hatched band in the color of the verdict. Softly highlight players in an offside position in red. For the car and the corner, the same graphic is green, because offside cannot be directly from them. Graphics appear and disappear smoothly.

Keep the text in one dark bottom bar: a short headline and one sentence, no more than 13 words in total including names. Explain mainly with the image and don't reveal the verdict before the viewer sees it. The names Vašek and Karel follow the characters as in a football game, they must not cover the players, the lines or the ball, and they blend seamlessly between positions.

6. INSPECTION AND DELIVERY

First, fine-tune one representative shot including movement, then the entire video. Write automatic checks: rules in each chapter, shot composition, word count, caption collisions, ball out of the boot, non-sliding footwork and determinism. View image sequences in detail and have the result independently reviewed (appearance, animation, clarity, technical errors); fix problems found and verify again. Check the finished MP4, not just the browser preview. Attach the source files with a short tutorial and clean up the working files.

pluvio9yte-099d1d.en:
1. Choose footage

  Three criteria that directly decide success or failure:

  - Complete subject: the person or object is fully in frame. Detail gets lost in processing and viewers recognize things by their silhouette; a close-up turns into a blob.
  - Clean background: solid color, snow, or sky all work, so the subject separates easily from the background.
  - Clear moments of action: strikes, jumps, landings, turns. These are the anchor points for the effects later on.

  The source can be your own footage, video-model output, or licensed existing clips.

  2. Break down the footage

  Extract three kinds of information from every frame:

  - Color: the original image.
  - Depth: how far each position is from the camera, computed with an off-the-shelf depth estimation model.
  - Subject area: where the subject is and where the background is.

  Also find the moments where shot changes happen. The key to this step is stability: depth and subject area must be processed consistently within each shot, otherwise playback will jitter.

  3. Decide the "particles" and "styles"

  First decide what to rebuild the image with: dots, squares, text, or lines all work.

  Then design a few styles. Each style is really just a different combination of three rules:

  - Where to place: across the whole frame, or only on the subject.
  - How big: uniform size, or varying with brightness and depth.
  - What color: the original image's colors, or one or two uniform colors.

  Add one more toggle: lay them flat on a single plane, or push them into 3D space by depth. Only once they're pushed in can the camera orbit.

  Four to six clearly distinct styles are enough. Particle density needs to be tuned by eye: too big and the content is unrecognizable, too small and it's no different from the original.

  4. Find the rhythm

  - Set the tempo: pick the music's tempo and slice time into equal-length cells. Make each cell an exact integer number of frames so every later switch lines up easily.
  - Find the action moments: combine two signals, "sound suddenly gets louder" and "image suddenly changes," to find the hit points in the footage.
  - Prepare the music: you can use an existing track and analyze its beats, or synthesize one at the chosen tempo and add accents on the hit points.

  5. Arrange

  Make a timetable specifying which style, which color palette, and where the camera is for each cell. Store this table separately; to adjust the rhythm later, only change it.

  Four principles of arrangement:

  - Establish the transformation at the start: show the original image first, then transition into particles, so viewers understand what's happening.
  - Alternate fast and slow: constant speed numbs the viewer; there needs to be a clearly slower section in the middle.
  - Colors should clash: the bigger the contrast in color and style between adjacent cells, the more forceful the switch.
  - The ending needs closure: e.g. the particles grow bigger and bigger until they become color blocks, or return to the original image.

  6. Feedback at key moments

  Layer short, sharp reactions on the hit points, graded by intensity:

  - Light feedback on every hit: the particles deform briefly, the camera bumps.
  - Medium feedback only on heavier hits: some of the particles burst toward the camera.
  - Big feedback reserved for the heaviest one or two hits: time freezes, the camera orbits.

  The principle is weak and short. Only move some of the particles and finish within a few frames, otherwise the frame explodes into a mess and viewers can't see what the subject is doing.

  Working methods throughout

  - Test samples before the full piece: after finishing each stage, render a few frames to check the result, and only move on once confirmed. Render the full piece only at the very end.
  - For uncertain parameters, produce a whole row at once: e.g. for density, have the AI output five or six levels side by side and you pick.
  - Re-render only what you change: when adjusting a section, re-render only that section.
  - Make the AI look at the images itself: at every step, require it to open and look at the render output before reporting.
  - Fix all randomness: ensure the same settings produce the same render every time, otherwise you can't make incremental changes.

2. Limit colors to 3–4 and typefaces to at most 2, and write the reason in one line

- 0–2 sec: The hook. Grab attention in the first 0.5 seconds

- 10–13 sec: The densest climax

- Particles gathering and dispersing

- Overlap motion across scenes. The next motion starts before the previous one ends, so no seams are felt
- Align the main motions to a 0.5-second beat (equivalent to 120BPM)
- Place a 0.3–0.5 second "wind-up" just before each highlight to create contrast in intensity
- Whatever moment you pause on, it should hold up beautifully as a single still image

zhu185178-41d6a2.en:
Make me a 30-second 2D animated storyboard previs short, "雨站" ("Rain Station"), with benchmark-level image quality. Don't install HyperFrames/Remotion; write all the code yourself (Python + ffmpeg).

Story (24fps, 2.39:1, 4K): an elevated train platform on a rainy night. She wears a beige trench coat and holds a clear umbrella, standing on the near platform; across the tracks under a streetlight stands him, in a long dark-gray overcoat and a scarf.
1. 0–6.4s Close-up of raindrops on the clear umbrella → pull back, focus shifts to the far side revealing him (over-the-shoulder shot)
2. 6.4–9.4s Medium close-up of him: head down → looks up toward frame left
3. 9.4–12.4s Frontal close-up of her: blinks → recognizes him; a horn sounds in the distance
4. 12.4–17s Wide shot: the headlights arrive first, a 5-car train passes; in the gap after the first car he's still there, by the second he's gone
5. 17–18.8s Close-up of her with tears in her eyes, bands of light from the train windows sweep across her face, her hair blown by the wind
6. 18.8–22.4s The taillights recede, the opposite platform is empty; his lamp flickers a few times and goes out
7. 22.4–28.6s Her back view, focus pulls from the empty platform back to her; footsteps behind her, a black umbrella covers her head, she turns and looks toward the camera; male voice: “好久不见。” (“Long time no see.”), with subtitles
8. 28.6–30s Title on black: “雨站 / RAIN STATION”

Approach:
- Artwork: use GPT Image 2.5 to draw the wide shot, him, her, and the train (lead car/middle car/rear car). Characters always on a pure green #00FF00 background and key them out yourself (asking for a transparent background with a reference image gives a fake checkerboard). Keep all poses of the same character in the same session, editing continuously with the base image as reference; when changing poses, composite only the changed region.
- Image quality: use Real-ESRGAN x4plus anime 6B (the safetensors version on HF; write RRDBNet yourself, run on MPS) to upscale all artwork 4x; use Depth Anything V2 to estimate depth for the wide shot and do per-pixel parallax.
- Rendering: write your own 2.5D compositor. Place each layer at its true depth, with a pinhole camera moving at real focal lengths; do circular bokeh, focus pulls, 3D rain streaks, train motion blur, volumetric light, bloom and film halation, fine grain, and color grading. Use mesh deformation on characters for breathing, wind-blown hair tips, and umbrella shake, switching key poses Japanese-style "on twos." 4K supersampling, cache frame by frame to disk, and parallelize across 3 processes by time range (16GB RAM).
- Sound: real Mixkit sound effects (rain, rain on the umbrella, train, horn, footsteps); write a score keyed to story beats and render it with the Steinway piano and string samples built into Logic/GarageBand; dialogue with a Kokoro Chinese male voice; per-shot sound distance, loudness -16 LUFS.
- At every step, render preview frames and tile them into a contact sheet to self-check; fix issues before outputting the film. Deliver a 4K master and a 1080p sharing version.
